questionText: Solve: 2x − 9 = 5
hints: This is an equation: things were done to x to reach the number on the right. Work backwards, undoing one thing at a time.
Begin with the − 9. What is the opposite of taking away 9? Do that to both sides and see what 2x is.
A similar one: 4x − 1 = 43. Adding 1 to both sides gives 4x = 44. Then 44 ÷ 4 = 11, so x = 11.

stepByStep.text: To undo the − 9, add 9 to both sides. 5 + 9 = 14, so 2x = 14.
2 lots of x make 14, so one x is 14 ÷ 2 = 7.
Check by putting 7 back: 2 × 7 = 14, and 14 − 9 = 5. So x = 7.

misconceptions.A: 14 is 5 + 9, which is what 2x equals, not x. One more step is needed to find a single x.
misconceptions.B: Put 2 back in to check: 2 × 2 = 4, but 2x has to be 9 more than 5. So x must be bigger.
misconceptions.C: 12 is 14 − 2. Finding 2x = 14 was right, but 2x means 2 times x, and multiplying is not undone by taking away.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Add 9 to both sides to get 2x = 14, then 14 ÷ 2 = 7.

questionText: Solve: 2x + 10 = 24
hints: This is an equation: things were done to x to reach the number on the right. Work backwards, undoing one thing at a time.
Begin with the + 10. What is the opposite of adding 10? Do that to both sides and see what 2x is.
A similar one: 4x + 1 = 49. Taking 1 from both sides gives 4x = 48. Then 48 ÷ 4 = 12, so x = 12.

stepByStep.text: The left side is 2x with 10 added. Undo this by taking 10 from both sides: 24 − 10 = 14, so 2x = 14.
2 lots of x make 14, so one x is 14 ÷ 2 = 7.
Check by putting 7 back: 2 × 7 = 14, and 14 + 10 = 24. So x = 7.

misconceptions.A: This divides 24 by 2 straight away. The + 10 has to be undone before dividing.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Take 10 from both sides to get 2x = 14, then 14 ÷ 2 = 7.
misconceptions.C: 14 is 24 − 10, which is what 2x equals, not x. One more step is needed to find a single x.
misconceptions.D: 17 is (24 + 10) ÷ 2. The 10 is added to 2x, so undo it by taking away, not by adding.

questionText: Solve: 7x + 17 = 101
hints: Think of the equation as a balance. Whatever you do to one side you do to the other, and you undo the adding or taking away before the multiplying.
On the left, 17 is added to 7x. Undo that first, on both sides, to find what 7x equals.
A similar one: 3x + 4 = 19. Taking 4 from both sides gives 3x = 15. Then 15 ÷ 3 = 5, so x = 5.

stepByStep.text: The left side is 7x with 17 added. Undo this by taking 17 from both sides: 101 − 17 = 84, so 7x = 84.
7x means 7 times x. Undo the multiplying by dividing by 7: 84 ÷ 7 = 12.
Check by putting 12 back: 7 × 12 = 84, and 84 + 17 = 101. So x = 12.

misconceptions.A: 84 is 101 − 17, which is what 7x equals, not x. One more step is needed to find a single x.
misconceptions.B: Try 16 in place of x: 7 × 16 + 17 = 129, but it should come to 101. So x must be smaller.
misconceptions.C: Put 14 back in to check: 7 × 14 = 98, but 7x has to be 17 less than 101. So x must be smaller.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Take 17 from both sides to get 7x = 84, then 84 ÷ 7 = 12.

questionText: Solve: 7x − 9 = 26
hints: This is an equation: things were done to x to reach the number on the right. Work backwards, undoing one thing at a time.
On the left, 9 is taken away from 7x. Undo that first, on both sides, to find what 7x equals.
A similar one: 3x − 2 = 25. Adding 2 to both sides gives 3x = 27. Then 27 ÷ 3 = 9, so x = 9.

stepByStep.text: To undo the − 9, add 9 to both sides. 26 + 9 = 35, so 7x = 35.
7x means 7 times x. Undo the multiplying by dividing by 7: 35 ÷ 7 = 5.
Check by putting 5 back: 7 × 5 = 35, and 35 − 9 = 26. So x = 5.

misconceptions.A: Put 3 back in to check: 7 × 3 = 21, but 7x has to be 9 more than 26. So x must be bigger.
misconceptions.B: 35 is 26 + 9, which is what 7x equals, not x. One more step is needed to find a single x.
misconceptions.C: Try 2 in place of x: 7 × 2 − 9 = 5, but it should come to 26. So x must be bigger.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Add 9 to both sides to get 7x = 35, then 35 ÷ 7 = 5.

questionText: Solve: 5x + 6 = 61
hints: Think of the equation as a balance. Whatever you do to one side you do to the other, and you undo the adding or taking away before the multiplying.
Begin with the + 6. What is the opposite of adding 6? Do that to both sides and see what 5x is.
A similar one: 4x + 1 = 49. Taking 1 from both sides gives 4x = 48. Then 48 ÷ 4 = 12, so x = 12.

stepByStep.text: The left side is 5x with 6 added. Undo this by taking 6 from both sides: 61 − 6 = 55, so 5x = 55.
5 lots of x make 55, so one x is 55 ÷ 5 = 11.
Check by putting 11 back: 5 × 11 = 55, and 55 + 6 = 61. So x = 11.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Take 6 from both sides to get 5x = 55, then 55 ÷ 5 = 11.
misconceptions.B: Try 12 in place of x: 5 × 12 + 6 = 66, but it should come to 61. So x must be smaller.
misconceptions.C: Put 13 back in to check: 5 × 13 = 65, but 5x has to be 6 less than 61. So x must be smaller.
misconceptions.D: 55 is 61 − 6, which is what 5x equals, not x. One more step is needed to find a single x.

questionText: Solve: 5x − 8 = 7
hints: This is an equation: things were done to x to reach the number on the right. Work backwards, undoing one thing at a time.
On the left, 8 is taken away from 5x. Undo that first, on both sides, to find what 5x equals.
A similar one: 2x − 6 = 14. Adding 6 to both sides gives 2x = 20. Then 20 ÷ 2 = 10, so x = 10.

stepByStep.text: To undo the − 8, add 8 to both sides. 7 + 8 = 15, so 5x = 15.
5 lots of x make 15, so one x is 15 ÷ 5 = 3.
Check by putting 3 back: 5 × 3 = 15, and 15 − 8 = 7. So x = 3.

misconceptions.A: Put 1 back in to check: 5 × 1 = 5, but 5x has to be 8 more than 7. So x must be bigger.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Add 8 to both sides to get 5x = 15, then 15 ÷ 5 = 3.
misconceptions.C: 10 is 15 − 5. Finding 5x = 15 was right, but 5x means 5 times x, and multiplying is not undone by taking away.
misconceptions.D: 15 is 7 + 8, which is what 5x equals, not x. One more step is needed to find a single x.

questionText: Find x: 3x−7=8−2x
hints: This is an equation with x on both sides. The aim is to get all the x terms on one side and the plain numbers on the other.
Add 2x to both sides. That removes the x from the right side. What does the left side become?
A similar example: 4x − 6 = 14 − x. Add x to both sides: 5x − 6 = 14. Add 6 to both sides: 5x = 20. Divide by 5: x = 4.

stepByStep.text: Add 2x to both sides. The left side becomes 5x − 7 and the right side becomes 8.
Add 7 to both sides to find 5x.
Divide by 5.
Check: 3 × 3 − 7 = 2 and 8 − 2 × 3 = 2. Both sides match.
So x = 3.

misconceptions.A: 15 is the value of 5x. Divide by 5 to find x.
misconceptions.B: Put 1 in: the right side is 8 − 2 = 6, but the left side is 3 − 7, which cannot be 6. Collect the x terms first.
misconceptions.C: Yes! With x = 3 both sides equal 2.
misconceptions.D: Put 5 in: the left side is 15 − 7 = 8, but the right side is 8 − 10, which cannot be 8. Add 2x to both sides to begin.

questionText: Sum of 2 natural numbers = 16, difference = 8. Product?
hints: This is a sum and difference problem. Find the two numbers first, then multiply them.
Add the sum and the difference together. That gives twice the bigger number.
A similar example: two numbers have sum 30 and difference 10. 30 + 10 = 40, and 40 ÷ 2 = 20 is the bigger number. The smaller is 30 − 20 = 10. Their product is 20 × 10 = 200.

stepByStep.text: Add the sum and the difference to get twice the bigger number.
Halve it to get the bigger number.
The smaller number is the sum minus the bigger number.
Multiply the two numbers.
The product is 48.

misconceptions.A: This is 8 × 8. Two 8s add up to 16, but their difference is 0, not 8. Find numbers that are 8 apart.
misconceptions.B: Check the two numbers. They must add up to 16 and be 8 apart. Then multiply them.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The numbers are 12 and 4, and 12 × 4 = 48.
misconceptions.D: This is 16 × 8, the sum times the difference. Find the two numbers themselves first, then multiply them.

questionText: Find 'a' in equation: 6a+8=4a+18?
hints: This is an equation with the letter on both sides. Collect the letter terms on one side and the plain numbers on the other.
Take 4a away from both sides. How many a are left on the left side?
A similar example: 7a + 3 = 4a + 15. Take 4a from both sides: 3a + 3 = 15. Take 3 from both sides: 3a = 12. Divide by 3: a = 4.

stepByStep.text: Take 4a from both sides. That leaves 2a + 8 on the left and 18 on the right.
Take 8 from both sides to find 2a.
Divide by 2.
Check: 6 × 5 + 8 = 38 and 4 × 5 + 18 = 38. Both sides match.
So a = 5. That is not in the list, so the answer is none of these.

misconceptions.A: Put 13 in: 6 × 13 + 8 = 86 but 4 × 13 + 18 = 70. The sides do not match. Collect the a terms first.
misconceptions.B: 10 is the value of 2a. Divide by 2 to find a, then look at the choices again.
misconceptions.C: Put 8 in: 6 × 8 + 8 = 56 but 4 × 8 + 18 = 50. The sides do not match.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The equation gives a = 5, which is not one of the numbers listed.

questionText: If 8P+7=39, Q=P+3. Find value of (2P+3Q).
hints: This has three small jobs. Find P from the equation, use it to find Q, then work out the last expression.
Start with 8P + 7 = 39. Take 7 from 39 to find what 8P equals.
A similar example: 6P + 5 = 17 and Q = P + 4. Find 2P + 3Q. First 6P = 12, so P = 2. Then Q = 2 + 4 = 6. Last, 2 × 2 + 3 × 6 = 22.

stepByStep.text: Take 7 from 39 to find 8P.
Divide by 8 to find P.
Q is 3 more than P.
Now work out 2P + 3Q with P = 4 and Q = 7.
The value of 2P + 3Q is 29.

misconceptions.A: 21 is just 3Q. Add 2P as well, which is 2 × 4 = 8.
misconceptions.B: This is 3P + 2Q, with the 2 and the 3 swapped over. Multiply P by 2 and Q by 3.
misconceptions.C: Yes! P = 4 and Q = 7, so 2P + 3Q is 8 + 21 = 29.
misconceptions.D: Check each part. P = 4 and Q = 7, so 2P is 8 and 3Q is 21. Add those two.

questionText: Mishti has 97 pens, Manav has 11. Mishti gives some so she has twice Manav's. How many given?
hints: When one person gives pens to another, the total number of pens stays the same. Use the total to find how many each has at the end.
Add the two amounts to find the total. At the end Mishti has 2 shares and Manav has 1 share, so there are 3 equal shares.

A similar example: Asha has 50 stickers and Ravi has 10. Asha gives some so she has twice as many as Ravi. The total is 60. Three equal shares: 60 ÷ 3 = 20, so Ravi ends with 20. He gained 20 − 10 = 10, so Asha gave 10 stickers.

stepByStep.text: The total number of pens does not change.
At the end Mishti has twice as many as Manav. That is 3 equal shares, with 1 share for Manav.
Manav ends with 36 pens. He started with 11.
Check: Mishti is left with 72, which is twice 36.
Mishti gave 25 pens.

misconceptions.A: Try it: Mishti would have 84 and Manav 24. But twice 24 is 48, not 84. Split the total of 108 pens into 3 equal shares.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Mishti is left with 72 and Manav has 36, and 72 is twice 36.
misconceptions.C: Try it: Mishti would have 54 and Manav 54. They would be equal, but Mishti should have twice as many.
misconceptions.D: Try it: Mishti would have 62 and Manav 46. But twice 46 is 92, not 62. Split the total of 108 pens into 3 equal shares.

hints: You do not have to find x itself here. Look at how 6x is related to 3x.

A similar example: if 2x + 5 = 16, find 4x + 5. First 2x is 16 − 5 = 11. Then 4x is double that, which is 22. So 4x + 5 is 22 + 5 = 27.

stepByStep.text: Take 7 from 38 to find 3x.
6x is double 3x.

misconceptions.C: Check your steps. 3x is 31, so 6x is 62. Then add 7.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 6x + 7 comes to 69, which is not one of the numbers listed.

questionText: For N=8, which equation is true?
hints: An equation is true when both sides come to the same number. Here you test each equation by putting 8 in place of N.
Take the first equation. Work out the left side with N as 8, then the right side. Are they equal? Do the same for the others.
A similar example: is 5N − 6 = 2N + 9 true when N is 5? Left side: 5 × 5 − 6 = 19. Right side: 2 × 5 + 9 = 19. Both sides match, so it is true.

stepByStep.text: Put 8 in place of N in each equation and compare the two sides.
First one: 3 × 8 − 14 = 10, but 8 + 3 = 11. Not equal.
Second one: 44 − 4 × 8 = 12 and 3 × 8 − 12 = 12. Equal.
Third one: 62 + 3 × 8 = 86, but 11 × 8 + 2 = 90. Not equal.
The true equation is 44 − 4N = 3N − 12.

misconceptions.C: With N as 8 the left side is 86 and the right side is 90. They are not equal.

questionText: If m+n=18, n+p=24, m+p=36, find value of p.

questionText: Sum of two consecutive odd numbers = 16. Sum of their squares?

Check: the two numbers are 12 and 13.
The smaller number is 12.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The numbers are 12 and 13, and 12 + 13 = 25.
misconceptions.B: 13 is the bigger of the two numbers. The question asks for the smaller one.
misconceptions.C: Check: 11 + 12 = 23, which is less than 25.
misconceptions.D: Check: 14 + 15 = 29, which is more than 25.

questionText: Anil thinks of a number. He adds 6 to it, multiplies the result by 4 and gets 60. What number did Anil think of?
hints: You know the end and want the start, so work backwards, undoing each step.
The last thing Anil did was multiply by 4. Undo it: 60 ÷ 4.
A similar one: a number plus 5, then times 3, gives 36. Backwards: 36 ÷ 3 = 12, and 12 − 5 = 7.

stepByStep.text: Undo the last step, multiplying by 4.
Undo the first step, adding 6.
Anil thought of 9.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Working backwards, 60 ÷ 4 = 15 and 15 − 6 = 9. Check: 9 + 6 = 15 and 15 × 4 = 60.
misconceptions.B: 15 is the number before multiplying by 4. Anil had added 6 to get it, so take 6 away.
misconceptions.C: After 60 ÷ 4 = 15, the adding of 6 must be undone by subtracting, not by adding again.
misconceptions.D: This does the steps forwards starting from 60. Work backwards from 60 instead: undo the multiplying, then undo the adding.

questionText: Kabir and his sister Diya save ₹96 altogether. Diya saves twice as much as Kabir. How much does Kabir save?
hints: Think of Kabir's money as one share. Then Diya's money is two of the same shares.
Together they have 1 + 2 = 3 equal shares, and the 3 shares make ₹96.
A similar one: two friends have 60 marbles, and one has twice as many as the other. 60 ÷ 3 = 20, so the friend with fewer has 20 marbles.

stepByStep.text: Call Kabir's saving 1 share. Diya's saving is 2 shares.
The 3 shares together are ₹96.
Kabir saves ₹32.

misconceptions.A: This splits the money into two equal halves. Diya has twice as much, so there are 3 equal shares in all.
misconceptions.B: Well done! Kabir's one share and Diya's two shares make 3 shares, and 96 ÷ 3 = 32.
misconceptions.C: ₹64 is Diya's saving, which is two shares. Kabir has one share.
misconceptions.D: This divides by 4. Kabir has 1 share and Diya has 2, so there are 3 shares.

questionText: A teacher shares some toffees equally among 8 children. Each child gets 7 toffees and 5 toffees are left over. How many toffees did the teacher have?
hints: Work back to the start: the toffees given out and the toffees left over together make the total.
Find how many toffees the 8 children got: 8 × 7.
A similar one: 6 children get 9 sweets each and 4 are left. 6 × 9 = 54, and 54 + 4 = 58 sweets.

stepByStep.text: Toffees given to the children.
Add the toffees left over.
The teacher had 61 toffees.

misconceptions.A: 56 is what the children got. The 5 toffees left over were also part of what the teacher had.
misconceptions.B: The left-over toffees are added, not taken away, because they were with the teacher at the start.
misconceptions.C: This adds 8, 7 and 5. Eight children with 7 each means 8 × 7 toffees.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 8 × 7 = 56 toffees were given out, and 56 + 5 = 61.

questionText: The perimeter of a rectangular photo frame is 46 cm. Its length is 15 cm. What is its breadth?
hints: The perimeter is the distance all the way round: two lengths and two breadths.
Half of the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Find half of 46.
A similar one: perimeter 30 cm and length 9 cm. Half of 30 is 15, and 15 − 9 = 6 cm is the breadth.

stepByStep.text: Half the perimeter is one length and one breadth.
Take away the length.
The breadth is 8 cm.

misconceptions.A: 46 − 30 = 16 is the two breadths together. Halve it to get one breadth.
misconceptions.B: This takes away only one length. A rectangle has two lengths, so take away 30 cm, then halve what is left.
misconceptions.C: 23 cm is half the perimeter, which is one length and one breadth together. Take away the length of 15 cm.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Two lengths use 30 cm, leaving 16 cm for two breadths, so each breadth is 8 cm.

questionText: On a balance, 3 equal boxes and a 2 kg weight are on one pan. They balance a 14 kg weight on the other pan. What is the weight of one box?
hints: A balance stays level when both pans hold the same weight. So the boxes and the 2 kg weight together weigh 14 kg.
Take the 2 kg weight away from 14 kg to find what the three boxes weigh together.
A similar one: 2 equal tins and a 3 kg weight balance 13 kg. The tins weigh 13 − 3 = 10 kg, so each tin weighs 5 kg.

stepByStep.text: Both pans weigh the same, so 3 boxes and 2 kg make 14 kg.
Weight of the 3 boxes.
Share among 3 boxes. One box weighs 4 kg.

misconceptions.A: 12 kg is the weight of the three boxes together. Share it equally among the 3 boxes.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The boxes together weigh 14 − 2 = 12 kg, so each weighs 12 ÷ 3 = 4 kg.
misconceptions.C: After taking away the 2 kg weight, 12 kg is left for 3 boxes, not 2.
misconceptions.D: The 2 kg weight sits with the boxes, so it is taken away from 14 kg, not added.

questionText: Tara's mother is 3 times as old as Tara. She is also 24 years older than Tara. How old is Tara?
hints: Think of Tara's age as one share. Her mother's age is three of those shares.
The mother has 3 − 1 = 2 shares more than Tara, and those 2 shares are 24 years.
A similar one: a father is 4 times as old as his son and 27 years older. The gap is 3 shares, so one share is 27 ÷ 3 = 9, and the son is 9.

stepByStep.text: Tara's age is 1 share and her mother's is 3 shares. The difference is 2 shares.
The 2 shares are 24 years.
Tara is 12 years old.

misconceptions.A: This divides 24 by 3. But the 24 years is the gap between 3 shares and 1 share, which is 2 shares.
misconceptions.B: This divides 24 by 4. The difference between the mother's 3 shares and Tara's 1 share is 2 shares.
misconceptions.C: Well done! The gap of 24 years is 2 of Tara's ages, so Tara is 12. Her mother is 36, which is 3 times 12 and 24 more than 12.
misconceptions.D: 36 is the mother's age. Tara's age is one share, which is 12.

questionText: Sana buys 5 pens of the same price. She pays with a ₹100 note and gets ₹35 back. What is the price of one pen?
hints: First find how much Sana really spent. Then share that cost among the pens.
She gave ₹100 and got ₹35 back, so the pens cost 100 − 35.
A similar one: 4 erasers, ₹50 paid, ₹14 returned. The erasers cost 50 − 14 = ₹36, so each costs 36 ÷ 4 = ₹9.

stepByStep.text: Money spent on the pens.
Price of one pen.
One pen costs ₹13.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The 5 pens cost 100 − 35 = ₹65, and 65 ÷ 5 = ₹13 each.
misconceptions.B: This shares the ₹35 change among the pens. The pens cost what Sana spent, which is 100 − 35.
misconceptions.C: This shares the whole ₹100. Sana got ₹35 back, so the pens cost only ₹65.
misconceptions.D: The change is taken away from ₹100, not added to it.

questionText: An auto-rickshaw charges ₹30 for the first kilometre and ₹12 for every kilometre after that. Imran pays ₹90 for his ride. How many kilometres does he travel?
hints: The fare has two parts: a fixed charge for the first kilometre and the same charge for each kilometre after it.
Take away the ₹30 for the first kilometre: 90 − 30. That money pays for the other kilometres.
A similar one: ₹20 for the first kilometre, ₹10 for each one after, and a fare of ₹100. 100 − 20 = 80, and 80 ÷ 10 = 8 more kilometres, so the ride is 9 km in all.

stepByStep.text: Take away the charge for the first kilometre.
Kilometres after the first.
Add the first kilometre. Imran travels 6 km.

misconceptions.A: Well done! After the first kilometre ₹60 is left, which pays for 5 more kilometres, so the ride is 6 km.
misconceptions.B: 5 is the number of kilometres after the first one. Add the first kilometre too.
misconceptions.C: This divides the whole ₹90 by 12. The first kilometre costs ₹30, so take that away first.
misconceptions.D: The ₹30 for the first kilometre is taken away from ₹90, not added.

questionText: In these two sums, ★ stands for one number and ▲ stands for another number. ★ + ★ = 18 and ★ + ▲ = 14. What number does ▲ stand for?
hints: Start with the sum that has only one kind of shape in it.
★ + ★ = 18 means two equal numbers add to 18. Find ★ first.
A similar one: ★ + ★ = 12 and ★ + ▲ = 10. Then ★ = 6 and ▲ = 10 − 6 = 4.

stepByStep.text: Two equal numbers make 18, so find ★.
Put 9 in the second sum: 9 + ▲ = 14.
▲ stands for 5.

misconceptions.A: 9 is the value of ★. Put it into the second sum to find ▲.
misconceptions.B: This takes 14 from 18. First find ★ from the first sum, then use the second sum.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Two ★ make 18, so ★ is 9, and 9 + 5 = 14, so ▲ is 5.
misconceptions.D: This halves 14, as if both shapes were equal. Only the first sum has two equal shapes.

questionText: Half of a number, increased by 8, is 20. What is the number?
hints: Work backwards from 20, undoing each step in turn.
The last step was adding 8. Undo it: 20 − 8 gives half of the number.
A similar one: half of a number, increased by 5, is 14. 14 − 5 = 9 is the half, so the number is 18.

stepByStep.text: Undo the adding of 8.
12 is half of the number, so double it.
The number is 24.

misconceptions.A: 12 is half of the number. Double it to get the number itself.
misconceptions.B: After 20 − 8 = 12, the halving is undone by doubling, not by halving again.
misconceptions.C: The 8 was added, so undo it by subtracting: 20 − 8, not 20 + 8.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 20 − 8 = 12 is half the number, so the number is 24. Check: half of 24 is 12, and 12 + 8 = 20.

questionText: A farmer keeps hens and 6 cows. Together the animals have 44 legs. How many hens are there?
hints: A cow has 4 legs and a hen has 2. Take out the legs you already know about.
The 6 cows have 6 × 4 legs. Take these away from 44.
A similar one: hens and 5 goats have 36 legs. The goats have 20 legs, 36 − 20 = 16 legs are hens' legs, so there are 8 hens.

stepByStep.text: Legs of the 6 cows.
Legs left for the hens.
Each hen has 2 legs. There are 10 hens.

misconceptions.A: 20 is the number of hens' legs. Each hen has 2 legs, so halve it.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The cows have 24 legs, leaving 20 legs for the hens, and 20 ÷ 2 = 10 hens.
misconceptions.C: The 20 legs left belong to hens, which have 2 legs each, not 4.
misconceptions.D: This takes the number of cows from the number of legs. First find the cows' legs: 6 × 4.

questionText: Gopal is x years old. His sister is 3 years younger than Gopal. Their ages add up to 21 years. Which equation matches this story?
hints: Write each person's age using x, then add the two ages.
Gopal's age is x. His sister is 3 years younger, so think about whether to add or subtract 3 to get her age.
A similar one: Mala is y years old and her brother is 2 years older; together they are 20. Mala is y, her brother is y + 2, so the equation is y + y + 2 = 20.

stepByStep.text: Gopal's age is x.
His sister is 3 years younger, so her age is x − 3.
The two ages add up to 21, so the equation is x + x − 3 = 21.

misconceptions.A: 3x would make the sister 3 times as old as Gopal. She is 3 years younger, so her age is x − 3.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Gopal is x, his sister is x − 3, and together they make 21.
misconceptions.C: x − 3 is only the sister's age. The 21 years is both ages added together.
misconceptions.D: 3x means three times Gopal's age. The story has two ages to add: x and x − 3.

questionText: Six times a number is the same as the number itself increased by 35. What is the number?
hints: Picture a balance: six equal bags on one side, one bag and a weight of 35 on the other. Removing the same thing from both sides keeps it level.
Take one of the number away from both sides. Then 5 times the number equals 35.
A similar one: four times a number equals the number plus 27. Take one away from each side: 3 times the number is 27, so the number is 9.

stepByStep.text: Six times the number equals the number plus 35. Take one of the number away from both sides.
Now 5 times the number is 35.
The number is 7.

misconceptions.A: This shares 35 among 7. But taking one of the number from each side leaves 5 times the number equal to 35.
misconceptions.B: 35 is five times the number. Divide by 5 to find the number.
misconceptions.C: This takes 6 away from 35. Six times the number means 6 multiplied by the number.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Six of the number is one of the number plus 35, so five of the number is 35, and the number is 7. Check: 6 × 7 = 42 and 7 + 35 = 42.

questionText: A balance is level. On the left pan there are 5 equal tins and a 3 kg weight. On the right pan there are 2 of the same tins and an 18 kg weight. What is the weight of one tin?
hints: A balance stays level if you take the same thing off both pans. Use this to leave tins on one side only.
Take 2 tins off each pan. Now the left has 3 tins and 3 kg, and the right has just 18 kg.
A similar one: 3 jars and 2 kg balance 1 jar and 10 kg. Take 1 jar and 2 kg off each side: 2 jars balance 8 kg, so one jar weighs 4 kg.

stepByStep.text: Take 2 tins off each pan. Left: 3 tins and 3 kg. Right: 18 kg.
Take 3 kg off each pan. Now 3 tins balance 15 kg.
Share among 3 tins. One tin weighs 5 kg.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Taking 2 tins and 3 kg off each pan leaves 3 tins balancing 15 kg, so one tin is 5 kg. Check: 25 + 3 = 28 and 10 + 18 = 28.
misconceptions.B: 15 kg is the weight of three tins together. Share it among the 3 tins.
misconceptions.C: This adds the 3 kg and 18 kg weights. When 3 kg is removed from both pans, 18 − 3 = 15 kg is left on the right.
misconceptions.D: After removing 2 tins from each pan, 3 tins are left on the left, not 5. So 15 kg is shared among 3 tins.

questionText: Asha has 52 stickers and Bina has 28 stickers. How many stickers must Asha give to Bina so that both girls have the same number?
hints: The total number of stickers does not change when one girl gives some to the other. Think about what each should have at the end.
Find the total: 52 + 28. Then share it equally between the two girls.
A similar one: Ravi has 30 marbles and Sam has 18. Together they have 48, so each should have 24, and Ravi must give 30 − 24 = 6.

stepByStep.text: Total stickers.
Each girl should have half.
Asha must come down from 52 to 40. She must give 12 stickers.

misconceptions.A: 24 is how many more Asha has. If she gave all 24, Bina would then have more. Asha gives only half of the difference.
misconceptions.B: 40 is how many each girl has at the end. The question asks how many Asha gives away: 52 − 40.
misconceptions.C: Well done! Together they have 80, so each should have 40. Asha gives 52 − 40 = 12, and Bina then has 28 + 12 = 40.
misconceptions.D: 80 is the total number of stickers. Halve it to see what each should have, then see how many Asha must give.

questionText: A parking lot has only auto-rickshaws with 3 wheels each and cars with 4 wheels each. There are 10 vehicles and 34 wheels in all. How many cars are there?
hints: Imagine every vehicle is an auto-rickshaw and count the wheels. Then see how many wheels are missing.
10 auto-rickshaws would have 10 × 3 = 30 wheels. Each car has one more wheel than an auto-rickshaw.
A similar one: 8 vehicles, bicycles with 2 wheels and auto-rickshaws with 3, and 19 wheels. All bicycles would give 16 wheels; the 3 extra wheels mean 3 auto-rickshaws.

stepByStep.text: Suppose all 10 vehicles are auto-rickshaws.
Extra wheels that are really there.
Each car adds 1 extra wheel, so the 4 extra wheels mean 4 cars.
There are 4 cars.

misconceptions.A: 6 is the number of auto-rickshaws. The question asks for the cars.
misconceptions.B: This divides 34 by 4 as if nearly all were cars. But 8 cars and 2 auto-rickshaws would have 38 wheels.
misconceptions.C: Yes! If all 10 were auto-rickshaws there would be 30 wheels. The 4 extra wheels mean 4 of them are cars. Check: 4 × 4 + 6 × 3 = 34.
misconceptions.D: 5 cars and 5 auto-rickshaws would have 20 + 15 = 35 wheels, one too many.

questionText: Three friends collect shells. Jaya has twice as many shells as Bala. Chitra has 5 more shells than Bala. Together they have 45 shells. How many shells does Bala have?
hints: Call Bala's shells one share. Write the other two friends' shells using that share.
Jaya has 2 shares and Chitra has 1 share and 5 more. So 4 shares and 5 make 45.
A similar one: Anu has twice as many as Binu, Charu has 3 more than Binu, and together they have 27. Then 4 shares and 3 make 27, 4 shares are 24, and Binu has 6.

stepByStep.text: Bala has 1 share, Jaya has 2 shares, Chitra has 1 share and 5 more. That is 4 shares and 5.
Take away the extra 5.
Share among 4. Bala has 10 shells.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Without Chitra's extra 5 there are 40 shells in 4 equal shares, so Bala has 10. Check: 10 + 20 + 15 = 45.
misconceptions.B: 20 is Jaya's number, which is twice Bala's.
misconceptions.C: 15 is Chitra's number, which is 5 more than Bala's.
misconceptions.D: This shares 40 among 5. Bala's one share, Jaya's two shares and Chitra's one share make 4 shares.

questionText: The length of a rectangular garden is 3 m more than twice its breadth. The perimeter of the garden is 48 m. What is the length of the garden?
hints: Half the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Write the length in terms of the breadth.
Half of 48 is 24. The length is 2 breadths and 3 m, so length plus breadth is 3 breadths and 3 m.
A similar one: the length is 1 m more than twice the breadth, and the perimeter is 32 m. Half is 16 m, so 3 breadths and 1 m make 16 m; the breadth is 5 m and the length is 2 × 5 + 1 = 11 m.

stepByStep.text: One length and one breadth make half the perimeter.
The length is 2 breadths and 3 m, so 3 breadths and 3 m make 24 m.
Find the breadth.
The length is 17 m.

misconceptions.A: 7 m is the breadth. The length is twice the breadth and 3 m more.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Length and breadth together are 24 m. Three breadths and 3 m make 24 m, so the breadth is 7 m and the length is 2 × 7 + 3 = 17 m.
misconceptions.C: This uses the whole perimeter of 48 m for one length and one breadth. One length and one breadth make half the perimeter, 24 m.
misconceptions.D: This is twice the breadth. The length is 3 m more than that.

questionText: Raju and Sonu start with the same amount of money. Raju buys 3 notebooks and has ₹14 left. Sonu buys 4 notebooks of the same kind and has ₹2 left. What is the price of one notebook?
hints: Both boys had the same money. Compare what each bought and what each has left.
Sonu bought just one notebook more than Raju. See how much less money he has left.
A similar one: with the same money, Mina buys 2 pens and has ₹20 left, and Tina buys 3 pens and has ₹5 left. The extra pen cost 20 − 5 = ₹15.

stepByStep.text: Both started with the same money, so 3 notebooks and ₹14 equal 4 notebooks and ₹2.
Sonu bought 1 more notebook than Raju.
That one notebook used up the difference in the money left. One notebook costs ₹12.

misconceptions.A: This adds ₹14 and ₹2. Sonu's one extra notebook made his left-over money go down from ₹14 to ₹2, so subtract.
misconceptions.B: This halves ₹14. Compare the two boys instead: one more notebook, and ₹12 less left over.
misconceptions.C: The difference of ₹12 pays for just 1 extra notebook, not 2.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Sonu bought one more notebook and has 14 − 2 = ₹12 less left, so a notebook costs ₹12.

questionText: Neha spends half of her money on a book. Then she spends ₹30 on a pen. She has ₹45 left. How much money did Neha have at first?
hints: You know the end, so work backwards, undoing the last thing first.
The last thing Neha did was spend ₹30. Add it back to ₹45.
A similar one: Ali spends half his money, then ₹10, and has ₹25 left. 25 + 10 = 35 is half, so he had ₹70.

stepByStep.text: Add back the ₹30 spent on the pen.
₹75 is the half left after the book, so double it.
Neha had ₹150 at first.

misconceptions.A: This doubles ₹45 first and then adds ₹30. Work backwards in order: add back the ₹30 first, then double.
misconceptions.B: ₹75 is what Neha had after buying the book. That is half of her money, so double it.
misconceptions.C: This adds ₹30 twice. Add ₹30 once to get ₹75, which is half of her money.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 45 + 30 = ₹75 was left after the book, and that is half, so she had ₹150. Check: 150 − 75 − 30 = 45.

questionText: Asha and Bina both start with the same number. Asha adds 8 to it and then doubles the result. Bina doubles the number and then adds 8. How much greater is Asha's answer than Bina's answer?
hints: Try the two sets of steps with a small number of your own and compare the two answers.
Start with 1. Asha: 1 + 8 = 9, and doubled that is 18. Now work out Bina's answer for the same start.
Similar problem: Raj adds 5 then multiplies by 3, and Sam multiplies by 3 then adds 5. Starting with 2, Raj gets 21 and Sam gets 11, so Raj's answer is 10 greater.

stepByStep.text: Try the number 1. Asha: 1 + 8 = 9, and double 9 is 18. Bina: double 1 is 2, and 2 + 8 = 10.
Asha is ahead by 18 − 10.
It is the same for any start: Asha doubles the 8 as well, so her 8 becomes 16, while Bina adds only 8.
16 − 8 = 8, so Asha's answer is 8 greater.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Asha's 8 gets doubled to 16 while Bina adds only 8, so Asha finishes 8 ahead whatever the starting number is.
misconceptions.B: It is tempting to think the same two steps give the same answer. Try both orders with the number 1 and compare.
misconceptions.C: Asha's 8 does become 16 when it is doubled. But Bina adds 8 too, so compare 16 with 8.
misconceptions.D: This halves the 8. Asha doubles her 8, so work through both sets of steps with a small number.

questionText: The two digits of a two-digit number add up to 9. When the digits are swapped, the new number is 27 more than the first number. What is the first number?
hints: Use one clue to make a short list of possible numbers, then test each of them with the other clue.
List the two-digit numbers whose digits add up to 9: 18, 27, 36, 45 and so on. Swap the digits of each and compare.
Similar problem: the digits add up to 7 and swapping gives a number 9 more. From 16, 25, 34, 43 test each: 34 swapped is 43, and 43 − 34 = 9, so the number is 34.

stepByStep.text: Numbers whose digits add up to 9: 18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72, 81, 90.
The swapped number must be greater, so the tens digit must be the smaller digit: try 18, 27, 36 and 45.
Only 36 gives a difference of 27, so the first number is 36.

misconceptions.A: 63 and 36 are the right pair, but 63 is the bigger one. The first number must be the smaller, because swapping makes it grow by 27.
misconceptions.B: The digits add up to 9, but swapping gives 54, which is only 9 more. Test the other numbers whose digits add up to 9.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 3 + 6 = 9, and swapping gives 63, which is exactly 27 more than 36.
misconceptions.D: 27 is the difference given in the story. Its digits do add up to 9, but swapping gives 72, which is 45 more.

questionText: Ravi has 4 times as many marbles as Sonu. Then each boy wins 5 more marbles. Now Ravi has 3 times as many marbles as Sonu. How many marbles did Sonu have at first?
hints: Test a possible answer in the story: work out both boys' marbles before and after, and see whether both clues hold.
Suppose Sonu had 5 at first. Then Ravi had 20. After 5 more each they have 10 and 25. Is 25 three times 10? Then try another start.
Similar problem: Mira has 3 times as many stickers as Nita; after each gets 4 more, Mira has twice as many. Try Nita = 4: Mira = 12, and afterwards 8 and 16. 16 is twice 8, so Nita had 4.

stepByStep.text: Test Sonu = 10. Then Ravi has 4 × 10 = 40 marbles.
After winning 5 each, Sonu has 15 and Ravi has 45.
45 is 3 times 15, so both clues fit.
Testing 5 gives 10 and 25, and testing 15 gives 20 and 65. Neither pair is 'three times', so only 10 fits.
Sonu had 10 marbles at first.

misconceptions.A: Great job! Sonu had 10 and Ravi 40; after 5 more each they have 15 and 45, and 45 is 3 times 15.
misconceptions.B: 15 is what Sonu has after winning 5 more. The question asks how many he had at first.
misconceptions.C: 40 is the number of marbles Ravi had at first. The question asks about Sonu.
misconceptions.D: Test it: Sonu 5 and Ravi 20 become 10 and 25, and 25 is not 3 times 10. Try a bigger start.

questionText: A basket has some mangoes. Asha takes half of the mangoes and 1 more. Then Bala takes half of the mangoes that are left and 1 more. Now 3 mangoes are left in the basket. How many mangoes were in the basket at first?
hints: Start from the end of the story and undo each step, the last step first.
Before Bala took his share there were more than 3 mangoes. He took half and 1 more, so first put back the 1, then double.
Similar problem: Ria takes half of some sweets and 2 more, and 4 are left. Put back the 2 to get 6, which is the other half, so there were 12 sweets.

stepByStep.text: Work backwards. After Bala there are 3 mangoes. Put back his extra 1.
That 4 is half of what Bala found, so before Bala there were 8 mangoes.
Put back Asha's extra 1. That gives 9, which is half of the basket.
Double it. Check: Asha takes 9 + 1 = 10, leaving 8; Bala takes 4 + 1 = 5, leaving 3.
There were 18 mangoes in the basket at first.

misconceptions.A: This doubles first and then adds 1. Going backwards, the extra 1 mango was taken last, so put it back first and then double.
misconceptions.B: This doubles twice and then adds both extra mangoes at the end. Each extra mango must be put back before its own doubling.
misconceptions.C: This doubles twice but leaves out the 1 extra mango that each child took.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Going backwards: 3 + 1 = 4, doubled is 8; then 8 + 1 = 9, doubled is 18.

questionText: In a game, Kavya wins 5 points for every round she wins and loses 2 points for every round she loses. She plays 20 rounds and finishes with 65 points. How many rounds did she win?
hints: Every round is either won or lost, so the two counts add up to the number of rounds. Test a possible number of wins.
Imagine she won all 20 rounds: she would have 100 points. Think about what changes each time one win becomes a loss.

Similar problem: 3 points for a win, 1 point lost for a loss, 10 rounds and 18 points. All wins would give 30. Each loss lowers the score by 3 + 1 = 4, and 30 − 18 = 12, so there were 3 losses and 7 wins.

stepByStep.text: If Kavya won all 20 rounds she would have 100 points.
Each lost round takes away the 5 points she would have won and 2 more, so it lowers the score by 7.
She is 100 − 65 = 35 points below 100, so she lost 5 rounds.
Check: 15 wins give 75 points and 5 losses take away 10, leaving 65.
She won 20 − 5 = 15 rounds.

misconceptions.A: This is 65 ÷ 5. But 13 wins would mean 7 losses, which take 14 points away and leave only 51. She must have won more rounds.
misconceptions.B: Excellent! 15 wins give 75 points and 5 losses take away 10, leaving 65.
misconceptions.C: This adds the 20 rounds to the 65 points and divides by 5. Test it: 17 wins and 3 losses give 85 − 6 = 79 points.
misconceptions.D: 5 is the number of rounds she lost. The question asks how many she won.

questionText: At a stationery shop, 2 pens and 3 pencils cost ₹36. At the same shop, 2 pens and 5 pencils cost ₹48. What is the price of one pen?
hints: Compare the two purchases. Look at what is the same in both and what is extra in the second one.
Both purchases have 2 pens. The second has 2 more pencils and costs more. Use that to find the price of one pencil first.
Similar problem: 1 bun and 2 biscuits cost ₹10, and 1 bun and 4 biscuits cost ₹14. The 2 extra biscuits cost ₹4, so one biscuit is ₹2 and the bun is 10 − 4 = ₹6.

stepByStep.text: The second purchase has 2 extra pencils and costs 12 rupees more.
So one pencil costs 6 rupees.
In the first purchase the 3 pencils cost 18 rupees, so the 2 pens cost 18 rupees.
One pen costs 18 ÷ 2 = 9 rupees, so the price of one pen is ₹9.

misconceptions.A: ₹6 is the price of one pencil, a very good first step. Now use it to find the price of a pen.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The 2 extra pencils cost ₹12, so a pencil is ₹6; then 2 pens cost 36 − 18 = ₹18, and one pen is ₹9.
misconceptions.C: ₹12 is how much more the second purchase costs. It is the price of the 2 extra pencils.
misconceptions.D: ₹18 is the price of the 2 pens together. Share it between the 2 pens.

questionText: A teacher has between 20 and 40 children in her class. When they stand in rows of 4, 3 children are left over. When they stand in rows of 5, 2 children are left over. How many children are in the class?
hints: List the numbers that fit one clue, then check each of them against the other clue.
Numbers between 20 and 40 that leave 3 over in rows of 4 are 23, 27, 31, 35 and 39. Now test each of them in rows of 5.
Similar problem: between 10 and 20, rows of 3 leave 1 over and rows of 4 leave 1 over. Rows of 3 give 10, 13, 16, 19. In rows of 4, only 13 leaves 1 over, so the answer is 13.

stepByStep.text: Rows of 4 with 3 left over: the number is 3 more than a multiple of 4. Between 20 and 40 that gives 23, 27, 31, 35, 39.
Rows of 5 with 2 left over: the number must end in 2 or 7.
In the list, only 27 ends in 2 or 7.
Check: 27 is 6 rows of 4 and 3 over, and 27 is 5 rows of 5 and 2 over.
There are 27 children in the class.

misconceptions.A: 23 fits the rows of 4, with 3 left over. But in rows of 5 it leaves 3, not 2. Keep testing the next numbers.
misconceptions.B: 32 fits the rows of 5, with 2 left over. But in rows of 4 nobody is left over. Both clues must fit.
misconceptions.C: 35 fits the rows of 4, with 3 left over. But in rows of 5 nobody is left over.
misconceptions.D: Well done! 27 is 6 rows of 4 with 3 left over, and also 5 rows of 5 with 2 left over.

questionText: On a balance, 1 melon weighs the same as 2 mangoes and 1 guava together. Also, 1 mango weighs the same as 3 guavas. How many guavas weigh the same as 2 melons?
hints: Change every fruit into guavas, one swap at a time, so that only one kind of fruit is left.
Start with one melon: it equals 2 mangoes and 1 guava. Swap each mango for the guavas it equals.
Similar problem: 1 box weighs the same as 2 tins and 3 nuts, and 1 tin weighs the same as 2 nuts. Then 1 box is 4 nuts + 3 nuts = 7 nuts, and 3 boxes are 21 nuts.

stepByStep.text: 1 mango equals 3 guavas, so 2 mangoes equal 6 guavas.
1 melon equals 2 mangoes and 1 guava, which is 7 guavas.
The question asks about 2 melons.
2 melons weigh the same as 14 guavas.

misconceptions.A: Great job! One melon is 6 + 1 = 7 guavas, so 2 melons are 14 guavas.
misconceptions.B: 7 guavas balance one melon. The question asks about 2 melons.
misconceptions.C: This swaps the mangoes for guavas but leaves out the 1 guava that sits with them on the pan.
misconceptions.D: This counts only 1 mango in each melon. One melon balances 2 mangoes and 1 guava.

questionText: A number is as much greater than 36 as it is less than 86. What is the number?
hints: Picture the three numbers on a number line. Where must the unknown number sit between the other two?
The number is the same distance from 36 and from 86. First find how far apart 36 and 86 are.
Similar problem: a number is as much greater than 10 as it is less than 30. The gap is 20 and half of it is 10, so the number is 10 + 10 = 20.

stepByStep.text: The number is the same distance above 36 as it is below 86, so it is exactly halfway between them.
The gap from 36 to 86 is 50.
Half of the gap is 25.
Add this to 36. Check: 61 − 36 = 25 and 86 − 61 = 25.
The number is 61.

misconceptions.A: 50 is the gap between 36 and 86. The number sits in the middle of that gap.
misconceptions.B: 25 is how far the number is from 36 and from 86. Add it to 36 to find the number itself.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 61 is 25 more than 36 and 25 less than 86, exactly halfway.
misconceptions.D: This adds 36 and 86. The number must lie between them, so halve that total.

questionText: Two whole numbers add up to 12. When they are multiplied, the answer is 35. What is the difference between the two numbers?
hints: Find the two numbers first by testing pairs, then read again what the question asks for.
List pairs that multiply to 35, or pairs that add up to 12, and look for a pair that does both.
Similar problem: two numbers add up to 10 and multiply to 21. 3 × 7 = 21 and 3 + 7 = 10, so the numbers are 3 and 7, and their difference is 4.

stepByStep.text: Pairs of whole numbers that multiply to 35 are 1 and 35, and 5 and 7.
1 + 35 = 36, but 5 + 7 = 12, so the two numbers are 5 and 7.
The question asks for their difference.
The difference between the two numbers is 2.

misconceptions.A: Well done! The numbers are 5 and 7, and 7 − 5 = 2.
misconceptions.B: 7 is the bigger of the two numbers. Read the question once more: it asks for the difference between them.
misconceptions.C: 5 is the smaller of the two numbers. The question asks for the difference between the two numbers.
misconceptions.D: This is 35 − 12. First find the two numbers themselves, then subtract one from the other.

questionText: A shop sells pencils only in packs of 4 and packs of 7. Meena buys exactly 30 pencils. How many packs does she buy altogether?
hints: Test the possible numbers of the bigger packs one at a time, and see whether the rest can be made from the smaller packs.
Try 1 pack of 7: that leaves 23 pencils. Can 23 be made from packs of 4? Then try 2 packs of 7.
Similar problem: packs of 3 and packs of 5, exactly 19 pencils. With 2 packs of 5 there are 9 left, which is 3 packs of 3. That is 5 packs altogether.

stepByStep.text: Try the packs of 7 one at a time. With no packs of 7, 30 is not a multiple of 4.
1 pack of 7 leaves 23, 3 packs leave 9 and 4 packs leave 2. None of these is a multiple of 4.
2 packs of 7 leave 16, which is exactly 4 packs of 4.
So she buys 2 packs of 7 and 4 packs of 4.
Meena buys 6 packs altogether.

misconceptions.A: 2 is the number of packs of 7. She also buys packs of 4, and the question asks for all the packs.
misconceptions.B: 4 is the number of packs of 4. Add the packs of 7 as well.
misconceptions.C: Excellent! 2 packs of 7 and 4 packs of 4 make 14 + 16 = 30 pencils, which is 6 packs.
misconceptions.D: 8 packs of 4 hold 32 pencils, which is too many. She buys exactly 30, so some packs must be packs of 7.

questionText: When a number is divided by 8, the quotient is 9 and the remainder is the greatest remainder possible. What is the remainder when the same number is divided by 5?
hints: First rebuild the number from the divisor, the quotient and the remainder. Think carefully about how big a remainder can be.
A remainder is always smaller than the divisor. When dividing by 8, what is the greatest remainder?
Similar problem: a number divided by 6 gives quotient 4 and the greatest possible remainder, which is 5. The number is 6 × 4 + 5 = 29. Divided by 4, 29 leaves remainder 1.

stepByStep.text: A remainder must be smaller than the divisor, so the greatest remainder when dividing by 8 is 7.
Build the number from the divisor, quotient and remainder.
Now divide 79 by 5: 5 × 15 = 75, and 79 is 4 more than 75.
The remainder is 4.

misconceptions.A: This uses 8 as the remainder, which makes the number 80. A remainder is always smaller than the divisor.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The greatest remainder is 7, so the number is 79, and 79 is 4 more than 75.
misconceptions.C: This uses 8 × 9 = 72 and leaves out the remainder. Add the greatest possible remainder first.
misconceptions.D: 7 is the greatest remainder when dividing by 8. One more step: build the number and divide it by 5.

questionText: Sunita is 30 years old and her daughter Pari is 6 years old. In how many years will Sunita be exactly 3 times as old as Pari?
hints: Both of them grow older together, so the gap between their ages never changes. Use that gap.
Sunita is 24 years older than Pari, now and always. When one age is 3 times the other, the gap is 2 times the smaller age.
Similar problem: a father is 38 and his son is 8. The gap is always 30. When the father is 3 times as old, the gap is 2 times the son's age, so the son is 15. That happens in 15 − 8 = 7 years.

stepByStep.text: Sunita is 24 years older than Pari, and this gap stays the same every year.
When Sunita is 3 times as old as Pari, the gap is 2 times Pari's age.
So Pari's age then is 12, and Sunita's is 36.
Pari is 6 now, so that is 12 − 6 years from now.
Sunita will be 3 times as old as Pari in 6 years.

misconceptions.A: In 4 years Pari is 10, and 30 is 3 times 10. But by then Sunita is 34, not 30. Both of them grow older.
misconceptions.B: 10 is 30 ÷ 3. Test it: in 10 years they are 40 and 16, and 40 is not 3 times 16.
misconceptions.C: 12 is Pari's age when it happens. The question asks how many years from now that is.
misconceptions.D: Well done! In 6 years Sunita is 36 and Pari is 12, and 36 is 3 times 12.

questionText: A snail is at the bottom of a well that is 10 m deep. Each day it climbs up 3 m, and each night it slips back 2 m. On which day does the snail first reach the top of the well?
hints: Follow the snail day by day, and think carefully about the last day: once it reaches the top it does not slip back.
After each full day and night the snail is 1 m higher. Find the height from which one day's climb of 3 m reaches the top.

Similar problem: a well 7 m deep, climbing 3 m each day and slipping 1 m each night. The snail starts day 2 at 2 m and day 3 at 4 m. On day 3 it climbs from 4 m to 7 m, so it reaches the top on the 3rd day.

stepByStep.text: Each full day and night the snail gains 1 m.
On its last day the snail climbs 3 m and is out, so it only needs to start a day at 7 m.
Gaining 1 m each full day and night, it starts a day at 7 m after 7 days and nights.
On the next day it climbs from 7 m to 10 m.
The snail first reaches the top on the 8th day.

misconceptions.A: A gain of 1 m each full day and night does suggest 10 days. But on its last day the snail climbs 3 m and is out before it can slip.
misconceptions.B: On the 7th day the snail starts at 6 m and climbs to 9 m, just short of the top. Follow it one more day.
misconceptions.C: This shares 10 m into climbs of 3 m and leaves out the slipping back each night.
misconceptions.D: Excellent thinking! The snail starts the 8th day at 7 m and climbs 3 m to reach 10 m before night comes.

questionText: If m = 21, and n = 3 and m = n × p, find the value of m ÷ p.
hints: The letters stand for numbers, and one of them is not given. Find the missing number first, then do the division the question asks for.
Put the known values into m = n × p. It becomes 21 = 3 × p, so ask yourself what number times 3 makes 21.
Here is a similar one: if m = 18, n = 2 and m = n × p, then 18 = 2 × p, so p = 9. Then m ÷ p = 18 ÷ 9 = 2.

stepByStep.text: Put the numbers in: 21 = 3 × p. Since 3 × 7 = 21, the value of p is 7.
Now divide m by p, which means dividing 21 by 7.
The value of m ÷ p is 3.

misconceptions.A: Great job! p is 7, and 21 ÷ 7 = 3.
misconceptions.B: 7 is the value of p. The question asks for m ÷ p, so one more step is needed: divide 21 by 7.
misconceptions.C: 5 does not fit here. First find p from 21 = 3 × p, then divide 21 by that value.
misconceptions.D: 4 does not fit here. First find p from 21 = 3 × p, then divide 21 by that value.

questionText: Radhika went to a store and bought 24 pieces of fruits. She purchased three times as many oranges as bananas. On her way home she accidentally dropped twice as many oranges as bananas. She still took home 15 pieces of fruit. How many oranges were there when she reached home?
hints: This story has two parts: the fruits she bought and the fruits she dropped. In each part the oranges and bananas come in a fixed pattern, so think in equal groups.
Start with the 24 fruits she bought. For every 1 banana there are 3 oranges, so the fruits come in groups of 4. Find how many such groups make 24.

Here is a similar one: Meena buys 30 fruits, with four times as many apples as pears. Groups of 5 give 6 pears and 24 apples. She drops 9 fruits, twice as many apples as pears, so 6 apples and 3 pears fall. She reaches home with 24 − 6 = 18 apples.

stepByStep.text: Three times as many oranges as bananas means groups of 4 fruits: 3 oranges and 1 banana. There are 6 such groups in 24, so she bought 18 oranges and 6 bananas.
She took home 15 fruits, so she dropped 9 fruits.
She dropped twice as many oranges as bananas, so the dropped fruits come in groups of 3: 2 oranges and 1 banana. There are 3 such groups in 9, so 6 oranges and 3 bananas fell.
Take the dropped oranges away from the oranges she bought.
There were 12 oranges when she reached home. Notice that the 15 fruits at home are 12 oranges and 3 bananas, which is no longer three oranges for every banana.

misconceptions.A: 9 is the number of fruits she dropped altogether. The question asks for the oranges she still had at home.
misconceptions.B: 10 does not fit the story. Find the oranges bought, then the oranges dropped, and take one from the other.
misconceptions.C: 6 is the number of oranges she dropped. Take those away from the 18 oranges she bought.
misconceptions.D: Excellent thinking! She bought 18 oranges, dropped 6, and reached home with 12.

questionText: Karan has bought 5 paise and 10 paise stamps for a total of 55 paise. If he were to buy the same number of 5 paise stamps, but twice the number of 10 paise stamps, it would cost him Rs. 1 and 5 paise. How many 5 paise stamps did he buy?
hints: Two purchases are described, and only one thing changes between them. Comparing the two totals shows what that change costs.
Change Rs. 1 and 5 paise into paise first. Then find how much more the second purchase costs than the first; that extra money paid for the extra 10 paise stamps.

Here is a similar one: some 5 paise and 10 paise stamps cost 70 paise. With the same 5 paise stamps and twice the 10 paise stamps the cost is 110 paise. The extra 40 paise buys 4 more 10 paise stamps, so there were 4 at first, costing 40 paise. That leaves 70 − 40 = 30 paise, which buys 6 stamps of 5 paise.

stepByStep.text: Rs. 1 and 5 paise is 105 paise. The second purchase costs 50 paise more than the first.
The only change is that the 10 paise stamps were doubled, so the extra 50 paise is the cost of the 10 paise stamps he bought at first. That is 5 stamps.
In the first purchase the 10 paise stamps cost 50 paise, so only 5 paise was spent on 5 paise stamps.
5 paise buys just one 5 paise stamp. Karan bought 1 stamp of 5 paise; the 5 found earlier was the number of 10 paise stamps.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Five 10 paise stamps cost 50 paise, and the 5 paise left buys 1 stamp.
misconceptions.B: With 3 stamps of 5 paise, the 10 paise stamps would cost 40 paise, and doubling them would give 15 + 80 = 95 paise instead of 105 paise. Compare the two totals to find the 10 paise stamps first.
misconceptions.C: With 4 stamps of 5 paise, 35 paise would be left for the 10 paise stamps, and 35 paise cannot be made from 10 paise stamps. Compare the two totals to find the 10 paise stamps first.
misconceptions.D: 5 is the number of 10 paise stamps. The question asks for the 5 paise stamps, so see how much of the 55 paise is left for them.

questionText: If 12x − 40 = 2x, then the value of x is?
hints: This is an equation with the letter x on both sides. Collect the x terms together so that x appears only once.
12x − 40 is the same as 2x. So when 40 is taken from 12x, only 2x is left, which means 40 must be the difference between 12x and 2x.
Here is a similar one: 8x − 42 = 2x. The 42 taken away is the difference between 8x and 2x, which is 6x. So 6x = 42 and x = 7.

stepByStep.text: Taking 40 away from 12x leaves 2x, so 40 is the difference between 12x and 2x.
Divide 40 by 10 to find x.
Check: 12 × 4 − 40 = 8 and 2 × 4 = 8, so both sides match. The value of x is 4.

misconceptions.A: With x = 3 the left side would be 36 − 40, and 40 cannot be taken from 36, while the right side is 6. Collect the x terms to get 10x = 40.
misconceptions.B: With x = 1 the left side would be 12 − 40, and 40 cannot be taken from 12. Collect the x terms to get 10x = 40.
misconceptions.C: You got it! 10x = 40, so x = 4, and both sides come to 8.
misconceptions.D: With x = 5 the left side is 60 − 40 = 20 but the right side is 10, so the sides do not match. Collect the x terms to get 10x = 40.

questionText: At a society meeting there were 21 more women present than the men. If the total men and women at the meeting were 105, then the number of women present at the meeting were?
hints: This is a sum and difference problem. You know the total of two groups and how much bigger one group is than the other.
Set aside the 21 extra women by taking 21 away from 105. What is left is two equal groups: the men, and the same number of women.
Here is a similar one: a class has 60 children, with 10 more girls than boys. Taking away the 10 extra girls leaves 50, and half of 50 is 25 boys. So there are 25 + 10 = 35 girls.

stepByStep.text: Set aside the 21 extra women. The people left are men and women in equal numbers.
Half of 84 is the number of men.
The women are 21 more than the men.
There were 63 women at the meeting. As a check, 63 women and 42 men make 105 people.

misconceptions.A: Great job! There were 42 men and 21 more women than that, which is 63.
misconceptions.B: 42 is the number of men. The women are 21 more than the men, so add 21.
misconceptions.C: 21 is how many more women there were than men. It is the difference, so use it to find the two groups.
misconceptions.D: 84 is what is left after setting aside the 21 extra women. Halve it to find the men, then add the 21 back for the women.

questionText: If 19/★ + 17/★ = 2, then what same number does ★ represent?
hints: Both fractions have the same bottom number. Fractions with the same bottom number are added by adding the tops.
Add the two top numbers. Then think: that total divided by the star must equal 2.
A similar example: 13/★ + 11/★ = 3. Add the tops: 13 + 11 = 24. So 24 divided by the star is 3, and the star is 24 ÷ 3 = 8.

stepByStep.text: The bottom numbers are the same, so add the tops.
So 36 divided by the star equals 2. Divide 36 by 2 to find the star.
Check by putting 18 in place of the star.
The star stands for 18.

misconceptions.A: 36 is the sum of the two tops. With 36 on the bottom the total would be 1, not 2. Divide 36 by 2.
misconceptions.C: With 19 on the bottom, the total is 36/19, which is a little less than 2.
misconceptions.D: With 17 on the bottom, the total is 36/17, which is a little more than 2.

questionText: Find the value of x in the equation: 97 − 17x = 5x + 31
hints: This equation has x on both sides and plain numbers on both sides. The aim is to gather the x terms on one side and the plain numbers on the other.
Add 17x to both sides so that all the x terms are together on the right. The equation becomes 97 = 22x + 31.
Here is a similar one: 50 − 4x = 6x + 10. Adding 4x to both sides gives 50 = 10x + 10. Taking 10 from both sides gives 40 = 10x, so x = 4.

stepByStep.text: Add 17x to both sides. The left side becomes 97, and the right side becomes 22x + 31 because 5x and 17x make 22x.
Take 31 from both sides, which leaves 22x = 66.
Divide 66 by 22 to find x.
Check: 97 − 17 × 3 = 46 and 5 × 3 + 31 = 46, so both sides match. The value of x is 3.

misconceptions.A: With x = 11, 17x would be 187, which is more than 97, so it cannot be taken away. Gather the x terms to get 22x = 66.
misconceptions.B: With x = 5 the left side is 97 − 85 = 12 but the right side is 25 + 31 = 56, so the sides do not match. Gather the x terms to get 22x = 66.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 22x = 66, so x = 3, and both sides come to 46.
misconceptions.D: With x = 9, 17x would be 153, which is more than 97, so it cannot be taken away. Gather the x terms to get 22x = 66.

questionText: Tom has 100 marbles and four boxes. He puts the marbles in the four boxes such that each box has 2 more marbles than the one before. The total marbles in the first 3 boxes are:
hints: The boxes hold numbers that go up by the same amount each time. Find what is in each box first, and read carefully which boxes the question asks about.
Compare every box with the first one. The second has 2 more, the third has 4 more and the fourth has 6 more. Take all these extra marbles away from 100 to see what four equal boxes would hold.

Here is a similar one: 60 marbles go into three boxes, each with 3 more than the one before. The extras are 3 + 6 = 9, so 60 − 9 = 51 and 51 ÷ 3 = 17 in the first box. The boxes hold 17, 20 and 23, and the first two boxes hold 37 together.

stepByStep.text: Compared with the first box, the other boxes have 2, 4 and 6 extra marbles. That is 12 extra marbles.
Without the extras, 88 marbles are shared equally among 4 boxes, so the first box has 22 marbles.
The boxes hold 22, 24, 26 and 28 marbles.
The question asks about the first three boxes only, so leave out the 28.
The first 3 boxes hold 72 marbles altogether.

misconceptions.A: 60 does not match the boxes. Find the four boxes first, which are 22, 24, 26 and 28, and add the first three.
misconceptions.B: 80 does not match the boxes. Find the four boxes first, which are 22, 24, 26 and 28, and add the first three.
misconceptions.C: Excellent! The boxes hold 22, 24, 26 and 28, and the first three add up to 72.
misconceptions.D: 88 is what is left after taking away the 12 extra marbles. Share it among the 4 boxes to find the first box, then add the first three boxes.

questionText: If 15 − 3x = x − 9, then the value of x is?
hints: This equation has x on both sides, and on each side something is being subtracted. Keep the two sides balanced while you gather the x terms together.
Add 3x to both sides so that x is only on the right. The equation becomes 15 = 4x − 9.
Here is a similar one: 20 − 2x = x − 4. Adding 2x to both sides gives 20 = 3x − 4. Adding 4 to both sides gives 24 = 3x, so x = 8.

stepByStep.text: Add 3x to both sides. On the left the 3x that was taken away is put back, leaving 15. On the right, x and 3x make 4x, so 15 = 4x − 9.
Add 9 to both sides to undo the subtraction of 9. This gives 24 = 4x.
Divide 24 by 4 to find x.
The value of x is 6. The key idea is that things being subtracted are cleared by adding: adding 3x clears the 3x taken away, and adding 9 clears the 9 taken away.

misconceptions.A: 3 comes from subtracting where adding is needed: 15 − 9 = 6 and 3x − x = 2x. To clear the 3x and the 9 that are taken away, add them to both sides.
misconceptions.B: With x = 5 the left side is 15 − 15 = 0, but the right side is 5 − 9, which is not 0. Add 3x and then 9 to both sides to get 24 = 4x.
misconceptions.C: You got it! Adding 3x and 9 to both sides gives 24 = 4x, so x = 6.
misconceptions.D: 12 comes from dividing 24 by 2. Adding 3x to x gives 4x, so divide 24 by 4.

questionText: Find the value of the variable 'T' when 31 − T = 2T + 7
hints: This equation has the letter T on both sides. Gather the T terms on one side and the plain numbers on the other.
Add T to both sides so that T is only on the right. The equation becomes 31 = 3T + 7.
Here is a similar one: 40 − T = 3T + 4. Adding T to both sides gives 40 = 4T + 4. Taking 4 from both sides gives 36 = 4T, so T = 9.

stepByStep.text: Add T to both sides. The left side becomes 31, and the right side becomes 3T + 7 because 2T and T make 3T.
Take 7 from both sides, which leaves 3T = 24.
Divide 24 by 3 to find T.
Check: 31 − 8 = 23 and 2 × 8 + 7 = 23, so both sides match. The value of T is 8.

misconceptions.A: Great job! 3T = 24, so T = 8, and both sides come to 23.
misconceptions.B: 24 is the value of 3T. One more step is needed: divide by 3 to find T.
misconceptions.C: 12 comes from dividing 24 by 2. Adding T to 2T gives 3T, so divide 24 by 3.
misconceptions.D: 6 comes from dividing 24 by 4. Adding T to 2T gives 3T, so divide 24 by 3.

questionText: Find the value of a: a + 5 = 12
hints: An equation is like a balance with the same value on both sides. To find the letter, undo what has been done to it.
5 has been added to a to make 12. Undo the adding by taking 5 away from 12.
Here is a similar one: n + 4 = 13. Taking 4 away from 13 gives n = 9, and 9 + 4 = 13 confirms it.

stepByStep.text: 5 was added to a to get 12, so take 5 away from 12 to find a.
Check: 7 + 5 = 12, so a = 7.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 7 + 5 = 12, so a is 7.
misconceptions.B: 17 comes from adding 5 to 12. The 5 is already added to a, so undo it by subtracting.
misconceptions.C: 5 is the number being added to a. Ask what number plus 5 makes 12.
misconceptions.D: 60 comes from multiplying 12 by 5. The equation uses adding, so undo it by subtracting 5 from 12.

hints: Here x is a hidden number. It was multiplied, then something was added. Undo those two things in reverse order to find x.
First undo the + 10. Take 10 away from 85 to find what 5x equals.
A similar example: 2x + 7 = 25. Take 7 from both sides: 2x = 18. Divide by 2: x = 9.

stepByStep.text: 5 times x, plus 10, makes 85. Undo the + 10 first by taking 10 from 85.
So 5 times x is 75. Undo the times 5 by dividing.
Check by putting 15 back in.
So x = 15.

misconceptions.A: This is 85 ÷ 5. Take away the 10 first, then divide by 5.
misconceptions.B: 75 is the value of 5x, not x. Divide it by 5 to finish.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 5 × 15 + 10 = 85, so this value fits.
misconceptions.D: Put 20 in: 5 × 20 + 10 = 110, which is more than 85. So x must be smaller.

questionText: Find the value of b: b − 5 = 12
hints: An equation is like a balance. To find the letter, undo what has been done to it with the opposite operation.
5 has been taken away from b to leave 12. Undo the subtraction by adding 5 to 12.
Here is a similar one: n − 6 = 9. Adding 6 to 9 gives n = 15, and 15 − 6 = 9 confirms it.

stepByStep.text: 5 was taken away from b to leave 12, so add 5 to 12 to find b.

misconceptions.A: 12 is the number on the other side of the equals sign. That is what is left after 5 is taken away, so b itself must be bigger.
misconceptions.B: 60 comes from multiplying 12 by 5. The equation takes 5 away from b, so think about which operation puts it back.
